claims.title: Malformed LLM responses are silently discarded
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**Malformed LLM responses are silently discarded**

This `catch` turns any parse failure into an empty result with no signal that scoring data was lost. Because callers then persist `null` relevance/color values as if the model simply found nothing, debugging bad prompts, truncated responses, or upstream model regressions becomes much harder. This catch block could hide malformed JSON, unexpectedly wrapped responses, or other parsing bugs while producing apparently successful pricing output. At minimum, emit structured context or rethrow so the failure is observable.

claims.title: LLM/API failures are swallowed and converted into fake scores
claims.text:
🔴 **High**

**LLM/API failures are swallowed and converted into fake scores**

This broad `catch` silently masks any failure in the scoring loop and fabricates threshold-passing scores for every comp. Users will be confused when relevance filtering suddenly lets everything through after an API outage or prompt/runtime error, and maintainers lose the original exception needed to diagnose it. This catch block could hide `runText` transport/auth failures, rate limits, unexpected runtime exceptions in batching, and parser regressions. Please avoid substituting synthetic relevance data here without surfacing the underlying error; either propagate the exception or record an explicit failure state that downstream code can handle transparently.

claims.title: Out-of-range relevance scores are accepted as valid
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**Out-of-range relevance scores are accepted as valid**

`parseRelevanceScores` only checks that `score` is a finite number, but downstream filtering assumes the model returned the promised 0–10 scale. If the LLM emits `11`, `100`, or `-1`, sold comps can be incorrectly kept or dropped, and active comps will store misleading audit data. Since this parser is now the single normalization point, it should clamp or reject scores outside the expected range.

*Suggested fix:*

```suggestion
  for (const [idx, entry] of Object.entries(parsed)) {
    const score = entry?.score
    if (typeof score !== 'number' || !Number.isFinite(score) || score < 0 || score > 10) continue
    const color = typeof entry?.color === 'string' ? entry.color : null
    entries.set(Number(idx), { score, color })
  }
```

claims.title: JSON extraction stops at the first balanced braces even if they are not the scoring object
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**JSON extraction stops at the first balanced braces even if they are not the scoring object**

`extractJsonObject` now avoids the greedy-regex problem, but it still assumes the first `{...}` block anywhere in the model output is the payload you want. If the LLM prefixes the real response with prose that contains braces (for example `note: {draft}` or an example object) and then emits the actual JSON object, this function returns the earlier brace block, `JSON.parse` fails, and the whole batch is treated as unscored even though valid scoring data is present later in the same response. That makes the parser less robust than the surrounding comments suggest. Please either continue scanning for a later balanced object after a parse failure, or narrow the extractor so it only starts from a brace that can begin a JSON object payload.

claims.title: Extractor can lock onto a non-JSON brace pair before the actual payload
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**Extractor can lock onto a non-JSON brace pair before the actual payload**

`extractJsonObject` now stops at the first balanced `{...}` block anywhere in the response. That fixes the old greedy-regex failure mode, but it introduces a different one: if the model emits any prose with braces before the real JSON object (for example `Note {approximate colors only}. {"0": ...}`), this function returns the prose fragment, `JSON.parse` fails, and the valid scoring payload later in the response is discarded. Because `parseRelevanceScores` does not continue scanning after a parse failure, one stray brace pair can zero out an entire batch's scores.
